text: Merge two sorted arrays. nums1 has length m plus n: the first m are real, the last n are placeholder zeros. Store the merged result in nums1, in linear time.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. The result must go back into nums1 in place, and its spare room is at the tail. Both inputs are non-decreasing. So I can't naively fill from the front, because that would overwrite unread nums1 values.
Right. How do you avoid that?
Fill from the back. Take the larger of the two ends and drop it into the last free slot, moving inward. The write index stays ahead of the unread data, so nothing gets clobbered.

Let me weigh the options. A naive approach would concatenate and sort, which is m plus n times log of m plus n, and wastes the fact that both inputs are sorted. Filling from the front needs a backup copy of nums1, so extra space of size m. This problem reminds me of the merge step of merge sort, just run backwards: one pointer per array, always placing the larger value at the back. That's linear time and constant space, because the tail slots make it work in place.

Here's the plan. One: start l at m minus one, r at n minus one, and the write index i at m plus n minus one. Two: while both have values, write the larger one at i and step that pointer back. Three: copy over any leftover nums2. Two things worth flagging. The invariant i at least l always holds: i moves back every step, l only when I take from nums1, so a write never hits unread data. And I only copy leftover nums2; if nums1 has leftovers, they're already in place. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Let me write it. Three indices start at the back. While both arrays have values, if nums1 of l is strictly larger it goes to slot i, otherwise nums2 of r does, and the used pointer and i step back. Then one loop copies any leftover nums2. One detail worth flagging: there's no second loop for leftover nums1, because those elements are already sitting in their final sorted positions at the front. And on a tie the else branch takes nums2 first, which is fine, since equal values can go in either order.

Let's dry-run one, two, three plus three empty slots, merged with two, five, six. Expected one, two, two, three, five, six. The row that matters is the last one: two against two is a tie, so nums2's two goes into slot two, and r drops below zero. The loop ends, and the leading one, two are already correct. That matches. Corner cases: if nums2 is all smaller, nums1 runs out first and the second loop copies the rest. M equals zero just copies nums2. N equals zero has nothing to do.

Time is linear in m plus n, since each element is placed once. Space is constant: three indices, in place, no backup. One more thing: the trick is to fill from the end that has free room, which generalizes to lots of in-place array work. And to merge k sorted arrays instead of two, I'd swap the two pointers for a min-heap of the k heads.
Nicely done. Three things stood out: filling from the back to stay in place, the i at least l invariant proving no overwrite, and only copying leftover nums2. Good work.
